question.text: Which form should a senior citizen (aged 60 or above) submit to a mutual fund house to avoid TDS on dividend income, if their total income is below the taxable limit?

explanation.text: The Logic: Under the Income Tax Act, TDS is deducted on dividend income from mutual funds when annual dividend payouts cross the prescribed threshold (commonly Rs. 5,000 per AMC). Investors whose total taxable income is below the basic exemption limit can pre-emptively self-declare zero tax liability and stop the TDS. The two prescribed declarations are Form 15G (for resident individuals below age 60 / HUFs) and Form 15H (specifically for resident senior citizens aged 60 or above). A senior citizen therefore uses Form 15H. The Trap: "Form 15G" is the correct declaration only for individuals below 60 years of age, not for senior citizens. "Form 26AS" is a consolidated tax-credit statement that reports TDS already deducted — it does not stop TDS from being deducted. "Form 10F" is used by certain non-resident taxpayers claiming DTAA benefits, unrelated to the senior-citizen TDS exemption use-case. Note: The cited NISM Series V-B workbook page (125) supports dividend TDS at 10% above Rs. 5,000 but does not mention Form 15H or Form 15G by name. The framing above reflects general Income Tax Act practice for resident senior citizens.
